title: Adding Lucene-style ?q= query string search for alerts made the Postgres backend build WHERE clauses by str.format()-ing user search terms into SQL.

findings.explanation: Several places in to_sql() interpolate user-controlled token values directly into the SQL string without parameterization: (1) `self.tokens.field[0]` is inserted literally as a column/field name inside double-quoted identifiers (e.g. `"{self.tokens.field[0]}"`). A double-quote in the field name closes the identifier and allows arbitrary SQL injection. (2) `tokens_attr` is built by replacing '_' with 'attributes' in the raw attribute token and then directly embedded. (3) The `subquery` branch replaces `__default_field__` with a constructed string that could itself contain injected SQL. Unlike the value tokens (which are correctly parameterized), the field/column name tokens are never validated against an allowlist of known column names.

else:
                p = _next_param(params)
                params[p] = f'%{self.tokens.singleterm}%'
                return f'"{self.tokens.field[0]}" ILIKE %({p})s'

findings.suggested_fix: Validate all field/column name tokens (`self.tokens.field[0]`, `self.tokens.fieldname`, `self.tokens.attr`, `tokens_attr`) against a strict allowlist of known schema columns before embedding them in the SQL string. Any field name not on the allowlist should raise a ParseException. Do not rely solely on double-quoting as protection against injection, as a double-quote character in the input breaks out of the identifier.

findings.explanation: The diff only changes how parsed query strings and their parameters are handled (refactoring from string interpolation to parameterized queries). No new endpoints, resource fetches by user-controlled IDs, or authorization checks are introduced or removed.
